prompt: Give the ground tiles a material that uses a normal map so they react to the 2D lights.

config.plan_model: Agent-tool model parameter 'sonnet' (Claude Code sub-agent; the harness did not report the resolved model id)
config.how: one fresh general-purpose sub-agent per plan, reads a job file with project brief + the developer prompt, writes numbered plan (<=8 steps, no code) via Write; not Claude Code plan mode

plans.text:
1. Inspect the existing TileMapLayer and its TileSet to see which atlas texture the ground tiles use, their tile size, and whether any material or light setup already exists in level_01.tscn.
2. Create or obtain a normal map image that matches the ground tile atlas layout exactly (same dimensions and tile arrangement), so each tile has a corresponding normal map region.
3. Add the normal map to the atlas texture by turning the TileSet's source texture into a CanvasTexture, with the current atlas as the diffuse texture and the new image as the normal texture.
4. Check the CanvasTexture settings, such as specular and shininess, and leave them at neutral defaults unless the developer wants a glossy look.
5. Make sure the level has 2D lights, such as a PointLight2D or DirectionalLight2D, with appropriate range, energy, and light mask layers that cover the TileMapLayer's light mask.
6. Confirm the TileMapLayer's canvas item light mask settings and blend mode match the lights, and assign a CanvasItemMaterial only if a specific light mode is needed.
7. Run level_01.tscn and move a light around the ground tiles to verify the shading responds correctly, with no flipped normals or seams at tile borders.
8. Tune the normal map strength, light height, and any tile edge bleeding, then check that the Player and enemies still look correct under the same lighting.

1. Open level_01.tscn and the TileMapLayer's TileSet to confirm how the ground tiles are set up (atlas source, tile size, which tiles are ground) and whether any 2D lights or a CanvasModulate already exist in the level.
2. Prepare or generate a normal map texture for the ground tiles that matches the tileset atlas layout and tile size exactly, so each tile lines up with its normal data.
3. Import the normal map with settings suited to normal data (no sRGB color conversion, no lossy compression, filtering matching the pixel-art look) and keep it next to the tileset image.
4. Create a CanvasItemMaterial-compatible approach: in the TileSet atlas source, use a CanvasTexture resource that pairs the diffuse atlas texture with the normal map as its normal texture, and assign it as the atlas texture.
5. Set the CanvasTexture's specular and shininess options if desired, then verify the TileSet still shows the tiles correctly in the TileSet editor with no offset or scaling mismatch.
6. Add a PointLight2D (or DirectionalLight2D) to level_01.tscn with a suitable light texture, energy, and height, and place it near the ground so the effect is visible. Consider a CanvasModulate to darken the scene so the lighting is noticeable.
7. Run the level and check that the ground tiles shade according to light position, then compare against the Player and enemy sprites to ensure the lighting looks consistent and nothing else became too dark.
8. Tune normal map strength, light height, and energy, and check the result on all ground and platform tiles; commit the new texture and scene or tileset changes once it looks right.

1. Locate the ground tileset used by the TileMapLayer and its tile atlas texture, and confirm how the level scene and enemies currently handle lighting. Check whether any lights or light occluders already exist in level_01.tscn.
2. Create or obtain a normal map image that matches the ground tile atlas layout exactly (same size and tile grid), so each tile's normals line up with its diffuse art.
3. Attach the normal map to the ground tiles by giving the tile atlas texture a CanvasTexture resource, with the existing atlas as the diffuse texture and the new image as the normal texture. Point the TileSet atlas source at this CanvasTexture.
4. Check that no custom shader material on the TileMapLayer overrides the default lighting. If a custom material is needed, use a canvas item shader that reads the normal map and the light direction.
5. Add one or more 2D light nodes (such as a PointLight2D or DirectionalLight2D) to level_01.tscn, with sensible height, energy, and range, so the tiles have something to react to.
6. Run level_01 and check that the ground shading changes as the lights move or the player passes. Adjust the normal map strength, light height, and light energy until it looks right.
7. Verify that the player and enemies still look correct under the new lighting, and decide whether they need their own normal maps for visual consistency.
8. Check that the tile collisions and the level layout are unchanged, then save the scene and tileset resources.

1. Open the project and inspect the TileMapLayer and its TileSet to see how the ground tiles are defined, which atlas texture they use, and whether any material or lights already exist in level_01.tscn.
2. Prepare a normal map texture for the ground tileset atlas, with the same dimensions and tile layout as the diffuse atlas, and import it into the project as a regular texture (not as a normal-map-flagged import that would alter it).
3. Create a CanvasTexture resource that pairs the existing diffuse atlas with the new normal map, and set it as the texture of the TileSet's atlas source so the tiles keep their look while gaining normal data.
4. Check whether the ground tiles need a custom material at all; if the default lit canvas item shading is enough, rely on that, otherwise create a shader or CanvasItemMaterial and assign it to the TileMapLayer's material property.
5. Make sure the tiles are affected by lighting by confirming the TileMapLayer's light mask matches the lights, and that the layer is not set to unshaded.
6. Add or adjust a PointLight2D or DirectionalLight2D in level_01.tscn with a suitable texture, energy, and height so the normal map visibly shades the ground, and leave Player and enemies' lighting settings consistent with it.
7. Run level_01 and move the light and the Player around to verify the ground reacts correctly, checking for seams between tiles, flipped normals, and unintended darkening of other sprites.
8. Tune the normal map strength, light height, and ambient level for the desired look, then save the scene and tileset resources.

1. Inspect the existing ground TileSet on the TileMapLayer (tile size, atlas texture, whether it already has a material or lights nearby) and confirm the Godot 4 version and renderer in use.
2. Obtain or create a normal map image for the ground tileset atlas, with the same dimensions and tile layout as the diffuse atlas, and import it into the project.
3. Create a CanvasTexture resource that pairs the existing diffuse atlas texture with the new normal map texture, and set specular and shininess if wanted.
4. Assign the CanvasTexture as the texture of the ground tile atlas source in the TileSet, so every ground tile uses the normal map without changing tile coordinates or collisions.
5. Make sure the TileMapLayer's CanvasItem material and light mode are set to the default Normal-compatible mode, and not unshaded or light-only, so lights actually affect it.
6. Add at least one PointLight2D or DirectionalLight2D to level_01.tscn (with a sensible height and light mask) so the effect can be seen, and check that the light's cull layers include the ground's light mask.
7. Run level_01 and move the light around or move the Player past it to confirm the ground shading reacts correctly; adjust normal map strength, light height, or the normal map's Y-direction convention if the lighting looks flipped.
8. Check that the Player, enemies, and collision behavior are unaffected, and tweak tile edge bleeding or filter settings if seams appear.

1. Open level_01.tscn and the TileMapLayer, and inspect its TileSet to see how the ground tiles are defined, which atlas texture they use, and whether any lights or a CanvasModulate already exist in the level.
2. Create or obtain a normal map image for the ground tileset atlas, matching the diffuse atlas layout and tile size exactly so every tile lines up with its normal data.
3. Import the normal map texture into the project and confirm its import settings are suitable (no sRGB conversion or compression artifacts that would distort the normals).
4. Add a CanvasTexture resource that pairs the existing ground atlas as the diffuse texture with the new normal map as the normal texture, and assign it as the texture for the TileSet atlas source.
5. Check that the tile atlas coordinates, margins, and per-tile collision and other tile data still work after swapping in the CanvasTexture, adjusting the atlas source if anything shifted.
6. Ensure the level has at least one 2D light (PointLight2D or DirectionalLight2D) positioned to light the ground, adding one if needed and setting its height and energy so normal-map shading is visible.
7. Run level_01 and move the player and the light around to verify the ground tiles shade correctly, and that the player, enemies, and other sprites still look right under the same lighting.
8. Tweak the normal map strength, light height, and any material settings until the effect looks good, then save the scene and tileset and note the change for the team.

1. Open level_01.tscn and the TileMapLayer, and check which TileSet resource and atlas texture the ground tiles currently use. Confirm whether other layers or scenes share that TileSet, so the change affects only the intended tiles.
2. Prepare a normal map image that matches the ground tile atlas layout exactly, either by generating it from the existing tile art or by painting it by hand. Save it next to the atlas with a consistent naming convention and import it as a regular texture, not as a color image.
3. Create a CanvasItemMaterial-compatible setup by assigning a CanvasTexture to the TileSet atlas source, with the existing atlas as the diffuse texture and the new image as the normal map. Tune the specular and shininess settings if the tiles need a shinier look.
4. If per-tile control is needed beyond the CanvasTexture, create a shader material that samples the normal map, and attach it to the TileMapLayer's material property. Keep this optional and only use it if the CanvasTexture route does not give the needed look.
5. Add at least one PointLight2D or DirectionalLight2D to level_01.tscn so the normal map has something to react to. Set its energy, color, range, and light mask so it affects the ground layer.
6. Check the light mask and the layer's light settings so the TileMapLayer is lit, and decide whether the Player and enemies should also be lit for a consistent look. Adjust the CanvasModulate or ambient color so the lit areas read clearly.
7. Run level_01 and move the light around, and the player past it, to verify that the tiles shade correctly from all angles and that there are no seams between adjacent tiles. Check the tile edges and the flipped or rotated tiles in particular, since the normals may need adjusting.
8. Fix any visual issues found, then save the scene and TileSet, and note the new files so they get committed with the project.

1. Inspect how the ground TileMapLayer and its TileSet are set up in level_01.tscn, including the tile size, atlas texture, and whether any material is already assigned. Confirm which 2D lights (PointLight2D or DirectionalLight2D) exist in the level, since the normal map only matters if lights are present.
2. Author or obtain a normal map image for the ground tileset atlas that matches the atlas layout and tile dimensions exactly, so each tile lines up with its normal data.
3. Import the normal map with correct settings (no sRGB or color-space conversion, matching filter and mipmap options to the diffuse atlas) so the lighting values are read accurately.
4. Create a CanvasItemMaterial-compatible setup by assigning a CanvasTexture resource that pairs the diffuse atlas with the new normal map, and use it as the TileSet atlas texture (or as the texture source for the ground tiles).
5. If the atlas cannot use a CanvasTexture directly, create a shader material with a light-aware shader that samples the normal map, and assign it to the ground TileMapLayer's material property instead.
6. Add or tune 2D lights in level_01.tscn (energy, height, range, and blend mode) so the normal map response is visible on the ground and platforms.
7. Run level_01.tscn and move the Player and a light around to check that shading reacts correctly, and that the Player and enemy sprites still look right against the lit ground.
8. Adjust the normal map strength, light height, and any shadow or light-mask settings based on the result, then save the scene and tileset resources.

1. Locate the ground TileSet resource used by the TileMapLayer and inspect its atlas texture, tile size, and whether the project already has any lights or a CanvasModulate in level_01.tscn.
2. Obtain or create a normal map image that matches the ground atlas layout exactly (same dimensions and tile positions), and import it into the project alongside the diffuse atlas.
3. Decide the approach: either a CanvasTexture resource that pairs the diffuse atlas with the normal map, or a custom shader material that samples the normal map. Prefer the CanvasTexture route because it works with the built-in 2D light normal mapping with no shader code.
4. Build the CanvasTexture with the existing ground atlas as its diffuse texture and the new image as its normal texture, then assign it as the texture of the TileSetAtlasSource so every ground tile uses it.
5. If a custom look is needed beyond built-in lighting, create a ShaderMaterial and assign it to the TileMapLayer, or to specific tiles via a tile's material property in the TileSet.
6. Make sure the level has at least one Light2D (PointLight2D or DirectionalLight2D) positioned near the ground, with its height and energy tuned so the normal map shading is visible.
7. Run level_01.tscn and check that the ground shading responds as lights move, adjusting normal map strength or the light height if lighting looks flat or inverted.
8. Confirm the Player, enemies, and other sprites still look correct under the same lights, and save the changes to the TileSet and level scene.

1. Open level_01.tscn and the TileMapLayer, and identify which TileSet resource the ground and platform tiles use. Check whether a normal map texture for the tileset atlas already exists.
2. Create or obtain a normal map image that matches the ground tileset atlas exactly (same dimensions and tile layout). Import it into the project and confirm it is imported as a regular texture, not as a color-corrected one.
3. Create a CanvasTexture resource that pairs the existing diffuse atlas with the new normal map, and assign it as the tileset atlas texture so the tiles keep their current appearance. Check the tiles still line up with their atlas coordinates.
4. Decide whether any custom material is actually needed; the default CanvasItem material with a CanvasTexture normal map is enough for Light2D to shade the tiles. Only add a material to the TileMapLayer if a custom shader effect is wanted.
5. Make sure level_01.tscn has at least one Light2D (PointLight2D or DirectionalLight2D) whose range and light mask include the TileMapLayer's light layer. Add one if missing, and tune its energy and height so the normal map is visible.
6. Check the TileMapLayer's canvas item settings (light mask, z-index, and any parent CanvasModulate) so lighting is not darkened or skipped. Adjust the CanvasModulate color if the scene is too dark.
7. Run level_01.tscn and move the Player past the light to confirm the ground tiles shade dynamically. Compare against the previous look and check for seams or tile-edge artifacts.
8. Tweak the normal map strength or light height until the effect looks right. Confirm the Player and enemy sprites still render acceptably alongside the lit tiles, and save the scene and resources.
